Title: Your Agent Passed the Prompt Test. Will It Survive Production?
Abstract:
A great prompt doesn't guarantee a reliable AI agent. What happens when your agent encounters unexpected inputs, real users, changing environments, or failures in production?

In this session, we'll explore why prompt testing alone isn't enough and how developers can test, monitor, and improve AI agents for real-world conditions. Learn how to move beyond getting the right response to ensuring your agents behave reliably, safely, and predictably in production.

Title: Prompting Is Not the System: Engineering Context, Contracts and Reliable Agent Behavior
Abstract: A prompt can influence a model, but it cannot replace an engineering system. When an agent has access to project context, tools, memory, and production workflows, reliability depends on the contracts around the prompt as much as on the wording inside it.  This talk moves from prompt-centric thinking to context engineering. We will examine a realistic agent workflow and identify where it breaks: incomplete or stale context, instructions that conflict with tool permissions, unstructured model output, retries that repeat side effects, and prompts that grow until nobody understands what the agent is actually allowed to do.  The session presents a practical model for reliable agent behavior:  - treat context as an explicit, versioned input contract; - separate stable policies, task context, retrieved knowledge, and user intent; - define tool schemas, permissions, validation, and failure behavior outside the prompt; - use structured outputs and deterministic handlers for decisions that must be predictable; - let the model reason where ambiguity exists, but keep high-risk actions behind policies and checkpoints; - evaluate complete workflows instead of judging isolated answers; - observe, test, and recover from failures in production.  Using AgentsKit as a concrete example, we will compare a prompt-only implementation with a bounded workflow that combines deterministic logic and model reasoning. The goal is not to eliminate prompts, but to put them in their proper place: one layer in a larger system of context, contracts, tools, evaluation, and operational feedback.  Attendees will leave with a practical checklist for diagnosing whether an agent needs a better prompt, better context, a stronger tool contract, or a different system design altogether.

Title: Whose gate is it?
Abstract: Every team running coding agents already has all three. A charter that says what the repository is about, a harness that decides how a turn happens, and a factory that decides how work ships. Almost nobody has drawn the lines between them, so a new rule lands wherever the person who noticed the problem happened to have commit access. Platform ships a harness and finds one team's opinion inside it. Development writes a charter and spends a third of it trying to configure a pipeline it cannot reach.  So I will put the levers on screen, context by context, and then walk a single rule down the six rungs where a gate can physically sit. Two more rungs sit off that chain, and both stay off it for a reason. On the way down, the context changes under you three times, and so does the team that owns the file.  Then the part platform engineers came for. There are two boundary lines here, and most designs only draw one. The context line asks what a thing governs. The ownership line asks who gets paged when it is wrong. Both lines agree at the charter, which belongs to development, and both agree at the factory, which belongs to platform. They cross inside the harness, which is where your org-design arguments have been living all along. You leave with that split named component by component, and with the rule that makes shared ownership survivable.

Title: Your Agent Can Write Terraform. It Can't Feel What It Breaks.
Abstract:
Prompt engineering decides what an agent intends. Something else decides what happens when it acts. An agent that can write and apply an infrastructure change has no way to feel that change's cost, latency or failure behavior until it's already live, and the usual guardrail, a sandbox, only covers code. It says nothing about what a workload does at 300 requests per second or what a node failure does to a queue.

This talk is about the missing layer between an agent's plan and the real cloud: a model of what the change will do. I'll simulate one proposed infrastructure change before merge and show the modeled CPU, latency, error rate, cost and resilience, then spend as much time on where the model is wrong as where it's right. I'll label every number as modeled, estimated or a known gap.

You'll leave with a way to give an agent consequences before it has access, and a clearer sense of which infrastructure questions a simulation can answer and which still need a real environment.

Title: Prompt Engineering for AI-Powered NEPA Compliance Automation
Abstract: Federal infrastructure, telecommunications, utility, and defense projects operating within historic districts and federally protected landmarks face complex environmental compliance requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). Analysts must evaluate regulatory thresholds across multiple federal agencies, often relying on manual review processes that increase permitting timelines and administrative workload.  This session presents a real-world case study of building an AI-powered permitting intelligence platform that automates NEPA Categorical Exclusion (CE) determinations for historically sensitive sites. The talk focuses on the prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and system architecture patterns used to support regulatory decision workflows while maintaining traceability and human oversight.  The platform integrates large language models, computer vision, geospatial intelligence, and regulatory knowledge retrieval across federal and state data sources, including Google Street View, NPS IRMA, FCC ULS, EPA ECHO, USGS 3DEP, and State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) systems. Attendees will see how structured prompts, multi-step reasoning workflows, and evidence-grounded retrieval strategies are used to analyze construction drawings, GIS boundaries, LiDAR data, imagery, and environmental records to evaluate CE thresholds such as ground disturbance, structure height increases, right-of-way constraints, and potential impacts on National Register-listed properties.  The presentation will cover practical implementation lessons, including prompt design for regulatory reasoning, retrieval grounding techniques, multi-source evidence synthesis, documentation generation, auditability, and human-in-the-loop validation. It will also discuss architectural decisions, integration challenges, and workflow automation approaches that reduced environmental data retrieval time and streamlined coordination across multiple agencies.  Attendees will leave with reusable prompt engineering patterns and system design approaches that can be applied to other high-stakes domains where accuracy, explainability, compliance, and operational efficiency are critical.

Title: Prompt Engineering for Agentic Safety Assurance in Physical AI
Abstract: Physical AI systems in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and other safety-critical domains continue to adapt after deployment, placing pressure on traditional engineering workflows. MBSE provides a strong foundation for requirements, architecture, verification, and traceability, but recent AI-assisted tooling has focused mainly on model generation, requirement checks, and use-case discovery rather than continuous safety assurance.  This session introduces a prompt engineering approach for Agentic Systems Engineering, where bounded, human-supervised AI agents support compliance monitoring, requirements traceability, hazard coverage assessment, operational design domain validation, and safety-case integrity. The MBSE model remains the single source of truth, while carefully designed prompts, structured outputs, validation rules, and escalation paths guide agent behavior.  Attendees will learn how to design prompt templates for evidence retrieval, requirement-to-hazard mapping, compliance checks, and exception reporting across ISO 26262, ISO 21448, UL 4600, and ASPICE. The talk also covers practical risks, including hallucinated evidence, incomplete context, prompt drift, and over-automation, along with controls that preserve human accountability. The result is a practical architecture for using prompts and bounded agents to strengthen continuous engineering assurance for next-generation Physical AI platforms.

Title: Prompt Engineering for AML: Building Reliable Compliance Workflows at Scale
Abstract: Financial crime compliance workflows are increasingly incorporating large language models to summarize transactions, interpret investigation context, generate analyst narratives, and support regulatory reporting. Yet in AML environments, prompt engineering cannot be treated as simple instruction writing. Prompts must operate against governed data, produce traceable outputs, handle incomplete evidence, and avoid introducing unsupported conclusions into compliance decisions. This session presents a practical prompt-engineering framework for building reliable AI-assisted AML and Currency Transaction Reporting workflows on top of cloud-native data platforms.  Drawing on patterns from large-scale financial data modernization, the talk explores how structured prompts, retrieval context, schema-aware instructions, validation layers, and reusable prompt templates can connect curated transactional data with downstream compliance applications. It examines techniques for grounding responses in approved data products, separating factual extraction from interpretive reasoning, controlling output formats, and designing prompts that fail safely when evidence is insufficient. The session also covers testing, observability, prompt versioning, and audit logging for production environments. Attendees will leave with practical design patterns for turning prompt engineering into a governed engineering discipline that improves consistency, reduces manual effort, and supports defensible financial crime operations.

Title: Why Single-Layer LLM Guardrails Fail: Lessons from Testing 390 Prompt Injection Attacks on AWS Bedrock
Abstract: Most teams protect their LLM applications with a single guardrail: a content filter, a system-prompt instruction, or one managed safety service. It looks fine in a demo. Then someone rephrases an attack, encodes it, or splits it across turns, and it gets through.  This talk shares what I learned building and testing guardrails for LLM and agentic AI systems on AWS Bedrock. I evaluated them against 390 attack prompts across 15 categories, including direct and indirect prompt injection, role-play jailbreaks, encoding and obfuscation tricks, and attempts to trigger destructive actions through an agent's tools.  We'll cover: - Why a single detection layer fails, and which attack categories get past it most easily - A dual-detection pattern that combines a managed guardrail with an independent second check, so each covers the other's blind spots - How to extend that into a layered architecture for AI agents, where catching a harmful action before it executes matters more than catching bad text - The tradeoff between false positives and false negatives, and why blocking too much is a real production failure too - An honest evaluation lesson: my first results file looked clean, but it turned out to contain only API throttling errors, not real model responses. How I caught it, and how to build an evaluation harness that won't fool you the same way.

Title: From 150K to 22K Tokens: Context Engineering for MCP Tool-Calling
Abstract: MCP made it trivial to give an LLM hundreds of tools - and quietly catastrophic for your context window. Every pre-loaded tool schema is prompt real estate, and in our production setup, the model was burning 150K tokens "before reading the user's question". Worse than the cost: tool-selection accuracy collapsed under the noise, with the model picking the right tool only 42% of the time.  This talk covers Code Mode, a context engineering technique that replaces MCP's schema dump with typed API stubs the model reads like library code. Same tools, different presentation - and this presentation resulted in: 85% token reduction (150K to 22K), tool-selection accuracy up from 42% to 80%, and fewer round-trips per task.  I'll walk through how we measured the baseline (and why most teams never notice this problem), how typed stubs change what the model actually attends to, the failure modes we hit along the way - stub granularity, stale type signatures, when the model hallucinates methods that "should" exist - and when you should "not" use this pattern. You'll leave with a measurement approach you can run against your own agent the same day, and a simpler alternative if numbers are difficult to comprehend.  Everything shown is from a real production system, not a benchmark.

Title: What Running a front facing AI Agent Taught Us About Prompt Engineering
Abstract: Getting an AI agent to work in a demo is easy. Keeping it reliable once real customers are talking to it is a different problem. Real users ask things you never planned for, mix languages and tone, push the agent toward answers it shouldn't give, and occasionally have conversations that go wrong without anyone noticing.  In this talk, I share what we learned taking a customer-facing AI agent from pilot to production. We'll look at why a single large system prompt breaks down under real traffic, and how moving to a structured approach (intent detection, grounded tool calls, and clear handoff rules to humans) made the agent more predictable. I'll cover how we used real failures and escalations as our evaluation set, what we log on every conversation so prompt changes can be tied to actual outcomes, and the guardrails we added for topics where a wrong answer has a real cost.  Attendees will leave with a practical checklist for designing, testing, and monitoring prompts for any agent that talks directly to customers.

Title: From Prompt to Product: How I Used AI to Design, Build, Integrate, and Launch Real Apps
Abstract: Prompting is not the beginning of bringing your idea to life it starts long before your first prompt. This session will have attendees leaving with not just understanding the power of their prompt in development but also:  1.  How to create a repeatable process when building a product 2. Participants will understand how to go from novice prompt to expert 3. How to make sure your prompt keeps your product in scope and recognize when it hallucinates.  4. The attendees will leave with a sense of understanding how to use tools like Resend, OpenAi Realtime, APiIs, and other tools for integration and how they fit in the process.

Title: Observing AWS AgentCore with Datadog: End-to-End Observability for Autonomous AI
Abstract: AI agents are moving from experimental demos to production systems, reasoning over data, invoking tools, interacting with applications, and taking actions on behalf of the business. As these systems become more autonomous, traditional application monitoring alone is no longer enough. Engineers need visibility into not only whether an agent is running, but also what it is doing, which tools it is invoking, how models are behaving, and what each interaction costs.  This session presents a practical approach to end-to-end observability for autonomous AI using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Datadog. We will walk through a production-style AI agent running on AWS and trace a user request across the complete execution path — from agent orchestration and model interactions to tool invocations, downstream AWS services, infrastructure, and application telemetry.  Using Datadog APM, LLM Observability, Infrastructure Monitoring, Logs, and OpenTelemetry-compatible telemetry from AgentCore, we will demonstrate how AI-specific signals can be correlated with traditional application and infrastructure telemetry in a single operational view.  The session will show how observability can help engineers understand agent behavior, identify failed or unexpected tool calls, investigate latency and errors, detect abnormal token and cost consumption, and establish operational guardrails for production AI workloads.  Attendees will leave with a practical reference architecture and an SRE-oriented methodology for moving from simply deploying AI agents to operating autonomous AI reliably at production scale.

Title: Beyond Better Prompts: Designing Reliable Prompt Engineering Workflows for Production AI
Abstract: Prompt engineering is often presented as writing clever instructions for AI systems, but production environments introduce challenges that go far beyond prompt wording. Reliability, consistency, evaluation, security, context management, and workflow design become critical when AI systems move from experimentation into real applications.  In this session, I’ll explore prompt engineering from a practical systems perspective. We’ll discuss techniques for building reliable prompt workflows, structuring context, reducing inconsistent outputs, managing prompt evolution, and improving response quality through iterative design approaches.  The talk will also cover common mistakes teams make when deploying prompt-driven applications, including prompt drift, poor evaluation strategies, and over-reliance on manual experimentation.  Attendees will gain practical guidance on moving beyond isolated prompts and designing prompt engineering workflows that support scalable and maintainable AI applications.  Whether you're experimenting with generative AI or deploying LLM-powered systems in production, this session provides practical lessons and architectural insights that can be applied immediately.

Title: You Cannot Fix a Prompt You Cannot See Fail: Debugging the Plan, Not Just the Answer
Abstract: Prompt engineering for single turn prompts has a tight feedback loop: change the prompt, read the output, judge it. Multi step and agentic prompting breaks that loop. When a reasoning chain goes wrong you see a bad final answer, but not which step chose the wrong path. You are tuning a plan you cannot see.  I authored the plan operation for agent planning spans in the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai#97), accepted upstream in May 2026. It makes the reasoning step a first class, portable span, so you can watch a prompting strategy plan, not just its final output. This talk shows how to instrument the planning step, how to tell a planning failure apart from a tool failure, and how to turn that signal into a measurement loop for prompt iteration. I will walk a demo, built for this talk, that catches a planning fault a final answer check would miss.

Title: Personalizing RAG for Prompt-Driven Enterprise Analytics
Abstract: RAG can reduce hallucinated responses by over 60% compared with non-retrieval baselines, yet enterprise analytics systems often provide the same retrieval and response experience regardless of a user's expertise, role, or objective. This session explores how prompt-driven personalization can make enterprise RAG systems more useful for real-world analytics workflows.  The architecture combines three components: a User Profile Store, a Multi-Index Retrieval System, and a Personalized Generation Layer. Retrieval uses five specialized indices covering schemas, metric definitions, past queries, documentation, and curated SQL examples. Personalized re-ranking combines semantic similarity, user relevance, and recency, building on research reporting 10% to 31% improvements in mean average precision depending on query type.  The session demonstrates how retrieval context and generation behavior can adapt for three analyst personas. Senior data engineers can receive SQL-first responses, business analysts can receive narrative interpretations, and product managers can receive concise KPI-oriented summaries.  Drawing from production experience with a comparable system spanning SQL query history, dashboards, real-time analytics, and code notebooks at a billion-user-scale technology platform, the session also presents practical evaluation methods for retrieval personalization, response depth, format appropriateness, adaptation speed, and stale-profile detection.

Title: Beyond Basic RAG: Better Context for More Reliable Enterprise AI
Abstract: Prompt quality is only one part of building reliable AI systems. In enterprise environments, the quality of retrieved context, the freshness of knowledge, and the ability to govern information often have a greater impact on model responses than prompt wording alone. As Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) becomes the foundation for enterprise AI, designing effective retrieval pipelines has become essential for improving accuracy and consistency.  This session presents a practical five-axis framework for enterprise RAG systems covering ingestion, indexing, retrieval composition, grounding strategies, and governance. Based on a comparative study of approximately 25 academic, open source, and commercial implementations, including eight major enterprise platforms, the session examines how production systems differ from research prototypes and why capabilities such as ACL-aware retrieval, provenance tracking, and time-aware evaluation are increasingly important for trustworthy AI.  Attendees will also explore seven engineering challenges that continue to shape enterprise AI, including long-document grounding, retrieval across heterogeneous content, freshness through change data capture, confidentiality-preserving evaluation, multi-agent retrieval, and balancing latency with operational cost. Rather than focusing on prompt templates or a specific framework, the session provides a vendor-neutral perspective on designing knowledge systems that consistently deliver higher-quality context for enterprise AI applications.
